prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B016 as a single prize part for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange confirmed that nobody questions the science, the maturity or the clinical scale. The chain runs from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) in humans, through receptor biology and the wider gut-pancreas-brain physiology, to agonists with randomized outcome evidence. The only live question is the third seat, so I have tested it again against the arguments for Knudsen. The prize is for a discovery, and the identification of the active peptide is the step on which both the later pharmacology and the drug development depend. Holst and Drucker are the secure core. A single-achievement prize is cleaner than trimming B016 to make room for a second part, because no member has made a scientific case for a second part that is as strong as the case for B016 itself.
statement.case_against: The reservation remains attribution, and I hold it as a real one. Mojsov's priority for identifying and synthesising active GLP-1 is contested by the Habener group, who are not on the credited list, and the supplied record does not let the committee settle it. Sandberg is right that this should be decided on the documentary record of who identified and synthesised the active form and showed its activity, and not on patent history. If that record cannot be defended, the trio with Knudsen is the safer fallback, and I would accept it, because a contested name is a larger risk to the citation than a pharmaceutical engineering step that is excellent in its own right. The configuration also leaves out the engineering of long-acting analogues, and the citation wording has to say plainly that the prize recognises the physiology and the active peptide that enabled the therapies, not the medicines themselves.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen so that the prize spans the arc from physiology to a once-weekly drug, and says that Mojsov's contested priority does not settle the third seat in her favour.
responses.response: I agree that contested priority does not by itself justify choosing Mojsov, and I accept that the arc from hormone to once-weekly drug is why this is a medicine prize. Where I still differ is the criterion. The citation recognises a discovery, and the discovery that made the drugs possible is the active peptide and its physiology. Knudsen's acylation work is extraordinary engineering that depends on that discovery. The citation can still say that the physiology enabled the therapies, so the arc is acknowledged without a laureate seat. I keep Mojsov, and I move to Knudsen only if the committee cannot defend her record.

responses.point: Sandberg asks that the third seat be decided on the documentary record of who identified and synthesised active GLP-1(7-36), not on patent history, and asks that Habener be kept explicitly in view.
responses.response: I accept this and it sharpens my position. I treated Mojsov as credible but contested in round 1, and I should state the test: who showed that the truncated form is the active one, who synthesised it, and who demonstrated its insulinotropic activity. Habener's group is part of that story, but the credited list gives us Mojsov and not Habener, and we cannot add a fourth or fifth name. I will keep Mojsov on that basis and say plainly that this is a judgement on an incomplete record. I disagree on a different year: the other elements of the arc are settled, and delay would not resolve the priority question.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that a prize should carry the physiology through to therapy, so that Knudsen's acylated long-acting analogues are the step that made the biology matter to patients, and he accepts that the basic trio is defensible.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously, and I note that our long collaboration on dopamine neurons does not bear on this ballot. On the substance, I agree that the analogues are what patients receive. I think the committee can honour that through the citation, which links the discovery to the incretin-based therapies, without making company drug development the centre of the credit. If colleagues think this leaves the prize looking like an idea without a drug, I would hear that, but I still read the Nobel criterion as favouring the discovery over the product.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps the basic-discovery trio, citing the tradition of rewarding a physiological mechanism with therapeutic consequence as its proof, and flags that the CAR-T credit omits the originator of the chimeric receptor concept.
responses.response: I agree with the reading of the prize tradition. On the second part, your Eshhar point reinforces my view that B007 is a good alternative but not a safe second part this year. If we added it, B016 would have to give up a name, and then we would have two contested attributions instead of one. For that reason I keep B016 alone in my preferred configuration and B007 as an alternative.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius calls recognition timely, arguably overdue, and prefers a single-achievement prize built on the people who established the biology, while keeping cGAS-STING and CAR-T as alternatives.
responses.response: I agree that the timing is right and that a single part is the cleanest option. I also keep your maturity argument against B005 in mind. The mechanism is clear, but without clinical benefit the case is weaker than for B016 or B007. I still rank B008 as my second alternative, because the technology has had a decisive effect on neuroscience, and I would accept B005 as a reasonable third.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 form can be defended against Habener on the record in front of the committee, which I cannot verify from the supplied text.
Whether the citation wording is enough to acknowledge the long-acting analogues when Knudsen is not a laureate.
Whether the committee wants a second part, and if so whether B007 can be defended with June and Sadelain alone, given Eshhar and Rosenberg.
How six optogenetics names could be cut to three for B008 if it were ever raised to a prize part.
statement.conflict_note: No change. No specific conflict applies to any shortlisted ballot from the provided profile. I was a postdoctoral fellow with Paul Greengard, who is not a candidate, and the profile records about twenty co-authored works with committee colleague Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy. None of this concerns a shortlisted candidate or credited name. B008 is near my broader neuroscience field, and I have treated it only as an alternative and judged it on the written record.
